editorial.headline: Material Recovery Beyond the Usual Waste Stream
editorial.standfirst: This activity turns used rubber, textiles, glass, oils and other non-metal waste into secondary raw material, with national PMA access and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
38309 covers a practical, industrial corner of the circular economy: recovering other materials from used goods and waste so they can return as secondary raw material. The record describes work that may produce pieces, fragments or other secondary forms. Its scope is deliberately broad, including used rubber such as tyres, rubber waste processed into granules, used textiles and clothing recovered through mechanical or chemical processing, glass that is crushed, cleaned and sorted, used oil and cooking fat converted into secondary inputs, and food, beverage, tobacco, agricultural, fisheries and other non-metal waste processed for recovery.

That breadth matters because this is not a retail recycling story; it is a processing activity. The registered business is doing the work of sorting, cleaning, breaking down, recovering or transforming waste streams into usable inputs. The code can fit operators handling rubber, textile, glass, oil or other non-metal recovery, provided the activity stays within the record’s central idea: used material becomes secondary raw material rather than remaining waste. The scales open to it are also broad. The record lists Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar, so the activity is not framed only for large industrial players; it can also sit with smaller recovery operators if their actual business activity matches the scope.

Nationally, the PMA picture is clean. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In plain English, the national record treats this activity as open to a fully foreign-owned PMA structure. There is no basis in the slim record to add a special licence condition, capital threshold, operating timeline or additional ownership qualification. The important point is narrower and stronger: for this specific activity, the national PMA field is open, and the ownership ceiling shown in the record is full foreign ownership.

The Bali reading is also specific. The record does not mark this activity as blocked for PMA registration in Bali. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent, but this activity is not caught by that block in the supplied data. The honest conclusion is therefore straightforward: nationally open, 100% foreign-owned in the record, and not Bali-blocked by the moratorium field provided here.
